utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, shall we continue with our case? Before that, I should like the Office of the Prosecutor to introduce itself, to have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Marchesiello and Ms Erasmus, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, my name is Goran Mikulicic and with my colleague, Mr. Joka, we represent the Defence on behalf of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The interpreters are ready? In that case, we can continue with the testimony of Mr. Sivro, I think it was. (The witness entered court) Good morning, Sir. Do you hear me? You may be seated. I wish to remind you that you read a solemn declaration yesterday pledging to speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. You are today in the same -- under the same commitment, yes? Therefore, you are going to answer questions that are going to be put to you by the Prosecutor in continuation of yesterday's proceedings. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor. MEHO SIVRO (continued) Examined by MR. MARCHESIELLO (continued)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are in fact resuming the chief examination which had been stopped yesterday in the afternoon. May I please ask the Registrar to put on the ELMO the map that had already been introduced into evidence and which was shown yesterday to the witness? Can you hear me, Mr. Sivro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before resuming and in order to let the judges know where the -- the history, the story Mr. Sivro is going to tell us, will you please show on the map and sign and circle with the pen the area in which you were at the moment you were being taken away from the frontlines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were on the way from Jelinak to Strane, is it not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were first going from Jelinak towards Loncari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we left you yesterday in a very distressing and painful situation. You all, guards and prisoners as well, were fleeing away from what seemed to be a very heavy BiH shelling, so let us resume at that moment. You had already been in a way sentenced to death, because the commander of the guards you were under -- you were with, as you said yesterday, had told them to kill you and now the only problem was to choose the place where you should have been executed. Please, go on with your story now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After -- we escaped the first threat of death, so to speak, when we reached the house where I think their command was, we continued our way to Loncari, because this house was still in the village of Jelinak at the bottom of the village. When we started off towards Loncari from that house, the only thing I thought of was how to escape, because I heard orders being given up there to kill us in the village of Loncari in a place called Bare; whether it was some kind of a pool or wood called Bare, I did not know. When we had almost reached the village, the shooting started from HVO weapons -- whether it was an anti-aircraft gun or anti-aircraft machine-gun. It was still dark, and they probably could not see the tree and the bullets were hitting this tree and the shrapnel from these bullets started showering upon us. When I saw that the guard was the first to lie down, I took advantage of the opportunity and started to run, but I was third in the line and, when I turned around, I saw that the prisoner behind me was not there, but that he was running towards the right. I did not want to follow him, so I turned left, and I was going up a slope, and I was running. When I reached the top of this little hill, I saw large fields -- it was already dawning and I saw that it was wheat that was growing there. I ran across the wheat fields for about a kilometre, and, as they were on a slope, there were large fences between the fields so I jumped over them and, when I reached the end of those fields, I took a rest and I looked up and I saw two HVO policemen standing above me. I immediately raised my hands. One of them started shooting immediately, whereas the other one was calmer -- he asked me where I was from and he said, "So you have come here to slaughter our women and children" and I said that I had been captured and that I had spent time at the Kaonik camp, that I had not killed anyone, that I was a civilian. However, they were emphatic, they ordered me to lie down. I did. They took off my belt and tied my hands with it. They kicked me in my body and one of them, who had this rifle, hit me with the rifle butt on the head. I had my head fractured in 20 different places. Luckily the butt was covered with rubber at the end so that the blows did not inflict heavier damage and I remained alive. I begged them not to kill me and I do not know whom I have to thank, but anyway they took mercy on me and they did not kill me. They took me back to the village, because nearby was an additional unit that had come to the assistance and they wanted to boast of having captured me. Among those soldiers I recognised a number of them, but one in particular and I addressed him. He was from Novi Travnik. I begged him to help me since he knew me. He just waved his hand and said more or less, "Never mind." The father of this man used to work for me and I was his foreman in the past. Then they decided to take me to the command after all. I begged them to report to the camp that they had found me and to hand me over there, but they did not have time for that and they said that they would take me to the headquarters in the village of Strane, so we set off towards the village of Strane. At one point in time they told me to crawl, and the path was muddy, because trucks had probably passed along that track overnight and they forced me to crawl in the mud, but, as that is impossible to do, I had to lean on my head as well to be able to crawl and I think that I only covered three metres and then the soldier --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, did you have your hands tied up behind your back at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, my hands were tied all the time with my own belt behind my back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you arrived at Strane to the HVO headquarters and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wanted before that -- I did not finish the story, telling you how he stepped on my head. He tried to suffocate me in the mud. He probably thought that I was done for. This went on for 10 or 20 seconds but I survived. I probably inhaled some of that water or mud, and I felt I was choking. My lungs could not start working again before I managed to spit it all out. Anyway, we went on towards the village of Strane. We got close to the village in a copse and they said, "let us not take him like this", because my appearance was terrible, my head was fractured, my teeth were broken, I was dirty. The Muslims still had not left the village. They thought it better for them not to see me. They said, "let us kill him here anyway". There was a big oak tree there, and I stood against it and he fired 3 to 5 bullets, but the bullets did not hit me --they whizzed by my head 2 or 3 centimetres away. Of course, I wet my pants, my legs gave way under me. Then the soldier said, "I could have killed you, but I did not want to". I could not get up. He helped me get up. He took me out of this wood, and the village was nearby --the village of Strane. He ordered me to sing as I was entering the village and I sang, of course, and we reached the HVO headquarters in that village. In front of the building, I saw three soldiers and a half-roasted calf was leaning against the wall. The fire had not been extinguished yet. They were all drunk, there was no commander in the headquarters, so I had to wait for him to come to decide what he would do with me. In the meantime I asked who was the commander, because quite a number of these boys were in the same dormitory as me when I went to school in Zenica so I was hoping I could find someone who would help me. Then I heard the commander's name was Ivica Andrijasevic. That is how I knew his name. They came, all beat me, each and every one of them, but the worst beating was when they asked me, "what is the name of this State?". I said, "Bosnia Herzegovina", I said "Croatia", whatever I said, they beat me. I just could not remember to say that the name of the State was Herceg-Bosna. They beat me, they thought I was stubborn and I did not want to give them the name of the State. In the meantime a Muslim came by. They ordered me to crawl under a vehicle, a very old vehicle with the tyres that were flat and even a cat could not crawl under it, but they insisted and they kicked me but I just could not. Then I started begging them to kill me. I did not feel the pain so much anymore because I was all swollen by then, I was all numb. Then one of them, drunk as he was, asked the commander, "Let me slit the throat of a balija for once in my life". He said, "Go ahead, do it, but at the end of the village and make him dig his own grave first". He accepted this with joy. He took me along their frontlines to the end of the village. All of them beat me, but I remembered one more than the others, a blond fair man, who sort of encouraged me, who swore at them and cursed their Ustasha mothers for mistreating me. When I started believing he was going to help me, he kicked me, in between the legs. Of course I fell. I do not know for how long I lay there. He lifted me up and we resumed our way. Some soldiers followed us, probably to watch the spectacle of me being slaughtered. This soldier who was leading me took out a knife, and he --he had turned the blunt edge of the knife under my neck. Again, I wet my pants from fear. And that is how we reached the end of the village. I kept thinking of the horrible death awaiting me when he was going to slit my throat. He told me to turn around --I did --and he emptied his whole magazine. I just felt that I had been hit in the left arm. I stood there for a couple of seconds maybe. Whether I was dreaming or I really experienced something, and I heard a sound -- it seemed to me -- saying "run", and this soldier who had emptied his magazine, he wanted to recharge and fire again, but as he was drunk, he just could not fix his rifle properly. So I jumped up and I threw myself over a fence. As it was very cold that morning, the grass was totally white from the frost and, when I threw myself over this fence, it was as if I was wearing skis and I skidded across down the slope. The people who had come to watch started shooting, but by then, because this was a slope, I had already put quite a distance between us and they started shooting at me. At about 80 metres away there was another fence, I thought I would not be able to stop there, that I would hit against this fence, because I had gained a lot of speed, but it was as in a film, I managed to stop, to jump over the fence again, and I found myself among the houses of Gavro Katici. There is a petrol station there. I tried to cut off my arm there because I was still tied up. This arm was just hanging on the skin. But as I tried to break it off, the belt slipped away from my hands, so I rested a while and I saw that they were not following me. I realised that this was no-man's land and that is why they were not following me. I cleaned up a little bit, and I collected myself and ran across the road to the petrol station. I ran, but I heard shots. Because there was a clearing, and then I thought: what should I do? If I run to the left, where our territory was, the territory controlled by the BH army, an automatic rifle would be there waiting for me and, if I ran in their direction, then, again, I would probably reach Lasva before they noticed me. So I ran and close to Lasva they started shooting at me. I jumped into the Lasva River and wet, beaten up, my right hand would not function -- whether it was a cramp or what, I do not know. I had on me a thin raincoat and I had shoved it into my trousers and, luckily, it swelled up a little and it served like a balloon and helped me surface. I went along the left side of the Lasva, because I was afraid on the right-hand side they would see me and shoot me. The Lasva was bloody with my blood -- I must have been bleeding a lot -- and when I felt that my right arm was coming to again, I went as far as the bridge, about 200 or 300 metres down river. I got to the right bank, I got hold of a branch and got out. They continued firing, and, when I got out, it was probably the BH army that realised what was happening and I heard voices saying, "Hurry up, there is a sniper following you." I ran across the ploughed fields, I heard the shots whizzing past me, but, luckily, they did not hit me. The distance between the Lasva River and the railroad is about 500 metres. I heard voices saying, "Cross the railway track and rest there", and that is what I did. I rested for a while on the other side of the tracks and I was probably unconscious for a while and, when I felt I had the strength, I started climbing up towards the village of Merdani. By then I knew that I was exposed to the sniper fire, but I thought to myself: I will try and whatever happens will happen. I managed to reach the first house, and I kept hearing exchanges between members of our army -- there was somebody saying, "Do not run into that house, go to the fourth house" and I managed to reach the fourth house. There was a nurse waiting for me; she gave me an injection and after that I was transported to the Zenica hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your arm, did you recover it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had to undergo four surgeries. I think I can use it up to 60 per cent. I was also injured in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I have no other questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you wish to put any questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can we suspend for 5 minutes? I see the witness is in a difficult psychological situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, maybe we could have a 15 minute break then. (10.29am) (A short break) (10.50am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, we have deep respect for what you have been through. Are you able to continue? Are you feeling okay now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes -- yes, we can -- I do apologise to the court, but I just could not help it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We do understand. Mr. Mikulicic, do you wish to put questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my co-counsel, Mr. Joka, will be asking questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The floor is yours, Mr. Joka. Cross-examined by MR. JOKA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Mr. Joka, I am Defence counsel for the accused. First of all, on my own behalf and on behalf of my colleague, I wish to express our deep sympathy for what you have been through and for what you are suffering and, also, that we are glad to see that you are well now, and do believe that it is really from the heart. We will not have many questions for you. I just wish to confirm something and see if I have properly understood you. After your first escape, when you were first captured -- after which you were captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in understanding that you were detained in Kaonik and after that you asked to be returned to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did explain that. I explained to them that I was a detainee and that I came -- had come there to dig trenches and I begged them to take me back, or to call the prison, and I begged them to be returned to Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I have to ask you why you did that, why did you beg them to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I simply thought that there was no more life for me otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Thank you, no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Sivro, you have completed your testimony here. Thank you very much for having come here to the Tribunal. We wish you a safe return to your country and thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Prosecution, do you have another witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: The Prosecution will call its next witness, Mr. Edib Zlotrg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Do we have to apply any protection measures for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: None whatsoever. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Sir. Can you hear me? Would you please read the solemn declaration that the usher is tendering to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please be seated. Thank you for having come to the International Criminal Tribunal. You are now going to answer questions that will be put to you by counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Meddegoda. Mr. Meddegoda, the floor is yours. EDIB ZLOTRG Examined by MR. MEDDEGODA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the purposes of the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Edib Zlotrg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 21st of October 1953.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are Bosniak by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your religion is Islam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a forensic expert -- I work for the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you followed any courses in forensic science or forensic technology?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what courses of study have you followed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed two courses -- two 6-month courses -- to be trained as a forensic technician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you follow these courses of study?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what educational institution was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an institution belonging to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, today, to which police station are you attached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police station in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there you work as a forensic technician?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, since 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in 1993, where were you residing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vitez, in Marsala Tita Street, number BB.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date 19th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the day I was arrested by members of the Vitezovi unit, which was an HVO unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of the day were you arrested by the members of the Vitezovi unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested at 7.30pm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which members of the Vitezovi unit came to arrest you on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of them was a colleague of mine from the police station, who used to work in the communications section, and his name is Drazenko Rados.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he wearing at the time he came to arrest you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform and had a coat of arms on his sleeve with "Vitezovi" written on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the Vitezovi unit is -- or was at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Vitezovi members came to arrest you, did they say to you why you were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not -- they just insulted me. They cursed me, my State and they asked me how come I was not in Stari Vitez to defend Alija State and similar things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell this court what happened when they came to your house in Marsala Tita Street in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they entered the building, I happened to be at my neighbours on the second floor and we were watching news. There was a shelling of Zenica on that day and many civilians were killed in front of the department store. This colleague of mine came in and he attacked me -- he accused me of hiding from them, and it was impossible to hide from them in that apartment. So, from my neighbour's place, he took me to the fourth floor where I lived, together with another member of the Vitezovi unit and there they searched me. They asked me whether I had any weapons, because they knew I had weapons officially assigned to me, but, prior to that, I had handed over my weapons to the municipal headquarters of the Territorial Defence and I had a valid permission for that, a valid certification for that, which I produced to them and, again, they cursed me, my State, my President, and they wanted to know how come I was there, how come I was not defending my State in the place called Mahala, and that is how they referred to Stari Vitez, to the town of Stari Vitez. Then Drazenko was surprised that I was still alive and I said, "You can see for yourself, I am alive." So he told me to take my things with me and we left the building. They put me in a van, where there was some elderly men and, from there, we were taken to the Workers' University, to the basement of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that is the building which is called the Radnicki University building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell this court what this Radnicki University building was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a building with some offices -- offices belonging to the League of Communists, to the union -- there were also premises that were used for adult education and there was also a cinema hall there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were brought there, were there others already detained in the basement where you were brought to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That basement used to be the boiler room of the building, and it was crowded, so, from one end to the other, you really have to elbow your way through the room. It was completely crowded and I think that there were some 250 people there, maybe more, so, when I was brought in, I realised that there were many people I knew, many acquaintances, and they expressed their condolences to me because they heard my brother and my sister-in-law had been killed. But they were also laughing, because apparently they had heard that I was also killed, together with my wife, so they were actually glad to see me alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was fully crowded with about 250 people. To what ethnic group did these people belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you happen to know any of those persons who were detained at the time you were brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long did you -- were you detained in this basement of the Radnicki University building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since they kept bringing more people every -- all the time, the place became really crowded, so, after a few days, they offered to take a group of people to the cinema hall. There were no windows in the cinema hall, so I went to the cinema hall together with some other 50 or 60 detainees. It was maybe three or four days after we were detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember being taken out of this cinema hall during the period you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the 24th, at about 10pm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were others taken out with you on the 24th -- the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. There were two or three of us that were taken from the cinema hall and more people were brought from other camps, so there was a group of about 10 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know -- do you remember where you were taken to from that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took our names down, and they put us in a van, and transferred us to the village of Nadioci, to the location called "Bungalows", and we got off the van and the guards ordered us to march with our hands behind our back. The driver and the escort went to the Bungalow, and I heard my former colleague, Vladimir Santic, laugh at that time. He said something like, "I know him for a very long time, we are acquaintances", and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you spend at the Bungalow in Nadioci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed there for about an hour, an hour and a half and from there we were taken to Kaonik. Actually, at that time we did not know where we were, but when we got off the vehicle, we found a lot of civilians there, 50 or 60 civilians were already there and they told us that it was a camp -- the Kaonik camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what time was it when you reached the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- it must have been some time after midnight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe to this court what happened upon reaching the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived in Kaonik camp, the escort of the driver, who was a member of the HVO, gave the list with our names to the guard and they put us into a hangar. There was only one stove in that hangar, and in the right corner there was a row of wooden pallets and people were sleeping on them. Those who were not fortunate enough to have a pallet were -- had to walk around the hangar or try to warm themselves near the stove. From the conversation I had with people over there, I learned that there were some people who had been there for about 25 days -- people who were arrested while travelling on a bus, or a truck, and there were even some workers from the Bratstvo factory. Apparently they simply move the entire bus of people to the Kaonik camp. There were people from Busovaca there, from the village of Strane and other villages I do not know very well. But there were quite a few people from the vicinity of Busovaca. During my time in Kaonik, at the beginning of my time in Kaonik, there was a group of people who had just returned from trench digging, and they said that killings were quite usual and that people also often got wounded while trench digging. An elderly man whose name I cannot remember told me a story about a young HVO soldier who took a sniper rifle, put it on his shoulder and started firing after that -- in the direction of the BH army lines, and, after he reacted, apparently this young HVO soldier then went together with him to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not recall the name of this elderly man who narrated this story to you -- narrated this incident to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long were you kept in the hangar of the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the 25th -- until 10, 11, and that is when they came back to pick us up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they picked you up around 10 or 11 in the morning, were you taken anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were. Again, they put us into the Volkswagen van and they took us to the place called Kratine; they took us to Miroslav Cicko, who was in charge there, and we were supposed to dig trenches there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many people were taken in the Volkswagen van to the place called Kratine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 10 of us, but there was already one group of other people there, so there were about 15 or 20 of us at Cicko's location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who this Cicko is, or Miroslav, or Cicko is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do -- he is a member of the HVO Croatian Defence Council, who, in 1992, committed a crime in the village of Nadioci. He called Esad Salkic and I was in charge of the investigation on behalf of the BH army. On that occasion, members of the HVO police told us that Miroslav Bralo had been arrested and that he was in prison. There is a video recording of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you surprised to see Miroslav Bralo when you in Kratine that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. According to the information I had, he was supposed to be in prison, because he had committed a heinous crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he speak to the detainees who had been brought for trench digging, or did he address the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got there, he lined us up in sort of half a circle, and he stood in the middle and he said that we were not Muslims, that we had never been Muslims, and that we were Croats, that we no longer had our religious institutions, that everything had been demolished by them and that we would continue being Croats. So he said that he was having a kind of competition with a member of the HVO in Busovaca as to who will kill more Muslims, and apparently he had killed about 80 women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else did Cicko Miroslav ask you to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wanted us to learn to make the sign of the cross. He made us do it several times and he made one man from the previous group show us how to do that, and after about half an hour, when his training was supposed to finish, he came back to see whether we had learned how to make the sign of the cross. So, my group, all 10 of us, except for one gypsy, we all knew how to make the sign of the cross, but he did not, this gypsy man, so Miroslav Bralo came back and some 10 or 15 metres away from the command building, he took an axe and he turned the blunt part of the axe above the head of that person and he said, "If you cannot do it now, this is it", so that person was probably frightened and he managed to do it the right way, he managed to do the sign of the cross. So Miroslav Bralo made him do it 10 times so that this man would make a mistake so that he could kill him, but he managed to do it properly all 10 times, so finally he had to give up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Miroslav Bralo bragging about one particular killing that he had committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is the incident that happened on the 26th in the afternoon, as we were resting during the lunch break, while we were digging trenches at the line in front of the command building, an HVO patrol brought three men to that place and they handed them over to Miroslav Bralo. The only thing we could observe at that time was that those young men were crawling across the field, and that he was taking them somewhere. After we came back, the guards told us that those three young men were from the village of Loncari and that they were hiding in a house and that they were caught by a patrol and brought over there, so Miroslav Bralo apparently tied their hands behind their backs, and they -- he made them clean up the field, and they had to do it with their teeth and their mouth and, after that, he took them to a pond in the vicinity of the headquarters, and the guard told us that whoever is taken -- whoever was taken to the pond to that location will never come back; and, indeed, we never saw these three young men again. They were probably slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you have to dig trenches at Kratine, witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 25th, at 11 o'clock, we started, and we finished on the 26th at 10 o'clock, with short breaks for lunch, maybe one-hour breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I seek your Honours' permission to show to the witness an excerpt of Exhibit P4? It is a map of the area where he was taken to for trench digging. There are copies for your Honours and a copy for learned counsel for the Defence, your Honours. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please, Registrar, could you give us the number of the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please, go on, Mr. Meddegoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the map on the ELMO and, using the pointer, point out the place, to the place called Kratine to which you were taken for trench digging on the 25th of April? (Witness indicates on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please, using one of the highlighters on the table, circle that area and mark the area with the letter "A". (Witness marked photograph). I move that Exhibit P62 be admitted into evidence, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After trench digging, witness, until the 26th, the morning, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evening of the 26th, around 10 o'clock, I was returned to the cinema hall of the Workers' University, Radnicki University, in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst at that building, were you registered by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 27th, a delegation arrived. There was one on the 26th as well, and they registered all of us except -- everybody except our group, who was digging trenches on that day, so they came back on the 27th to take our names down as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were registered on the 27th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days thereafter did you spend in the Radnicki University building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed -- I stayed there until 30th of April, when the BH army commander, Sefer Halilovic, signed an agreement with the commander of the HVO, Petkovic, where it was agreed there would be an exchange on the principle all-for-all, so he came to the university and he said that we were free and that we would be able to go wherever we wanted to. However, the HVO police did not allow that to happen in my respect, because I used to be a member of the police, so I was simply returned to where I was before. However, this former colleague of mine, Zeljko Sajevic, he was a member of the staff of the local HVO brigade and he arranged for me to be released on 30th of April and that is when I went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there was an agreement signed between the BH commander Sefer Halilovic and Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what was told to us by Mr. Halilovic when he came to the cinema hall and spoke to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What rank did Petkovic have at the time he signed the agreement? Are you aware of what rank he held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what rank he held. I know he was the commander of the main staff, but I do not know what rank he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Commander of the main staff of HVO, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Petkovic was a Croat or a Bosnian Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before being released -- before being released from the Radnicki building, did you have to sign any papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had to sign a paper saying that I was leaving voluntarily, in one piece, safe and sound, and the president of the commission for the exchange of us prisoners on behalf of the HVO was Borislav -- I do not remember his surname -- he was a security officer in the special purpose industry in Vitez -- he was killed during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After being released on the 30th of April, for how long were you at liberty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 1st of May about 3pm, Anto Kovac and Jurcevic, whose name I do not remember but his nickname was Butur, he came to fetch me allegedly for a statement and I would be immediately released and they took me to the cinema hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Anto Kovac and Jurcevic, who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were members of the military police who were in charge of the security at the camp in the Workers' University, because the Workers' University had people detained in the basement, in the cinema hall and upstairs on the first floor. Anto Kovac I think was a commander of the platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To which army did they belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you were again taken to the Radnicki University building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you went there on the 1st of May, did you see others detained in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many others were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 50 or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe to this court what happened when you were brought to this building on the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the next day, on the 2nd of May, that Kovac Anto and Jurcevic came into the hall and told us all to go to the bottom of the cinema. The two of them sat at a table on the stage. They were sitting facing one another, one of them had a red agenda, the other one had a blue one and all of us had to go up to them, one by one, and to give our particulars, and they would enter them, for some people in the blue agenda and for others in the red one. There were five or six of us whose names were entered in the red agenda and we were later moved from the cinema hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you moved to, from the cinema hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With another six persons, who had been brought there from the premises of the SDK and the primary school, we were transferred to the premises of the chess club, which were close to my own apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, for how long were you detained at the chess club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A couple of days -- two or three days, until about the 5th, so two nights -- two nights and three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened on the 5th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 5th of May, in the afternoon, around 3pm or 4pm, a combi van was parked in front and we were told to get in and to leave our things and they drove us somewhere, we did not know where. When we reached our destination, the driver and co-driver left the van and we were surrounded by HVO members under full combat gear, helmet, flak jacket, long barreled rifles and they held us there for about an hour, an hour and a half. Later on, one by one, we were put in the prison -- first searched and the 13 of us were pushed into one cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you know now to which cell you were put in on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which cell was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately to the right, right next to the premises where the policemen on duty were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I seek your permission to show to the witness aerial photograph of the Kaonik camp? There are five copies for your Honours as well as for Defence counsel. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, looking at exhibit number 63, which is now on the ELMO, could you please, using the pointer, point out to the building where you were taken to on the 5th of May, the building with the cells? Could you please circle that building and mark it with the letter "B". (Witness marked photograph). Witness, you would also recall that you were brought to the Kaonik camp on your way -- on your way from Nadioci. You said you were brought to a hangar building. Do you see that hangar building on the exhibit that is on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please point out that building, the hangar building? (Witness indicates). Once again, using the highlighter, could you please circle that and mark that building with the letter "A"? (Witness marked photograph). Now, you said you were put into a cell with the others. How many others were put into your cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thirteen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which cell were you put into, you and the 12 others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the number exactly -- it was number 13 or 16, but it is the cell right next to the room where the guards were, which means when you enter the prison, to the right of the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I have your permission to show to the witness exhibit number 20, which has already been admitted into evidence? These are copies of that same exhibit, your Honours. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Once again, witness, could you look at Exhibit 64 and, using the pointer, try to identify the cell to which you were brought in on the 5th of May? (Witness indicates on photograph). Thank you. Could you please mark -- you can see the door of that cell; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please mark that door with the letter "A"? (Witness marked photograph). Witness, do you recognise any other object on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right next to us, this was the room where the guards were. There was a TV set in the corner, which could be seen when we had lunch, because I usually sat here on this side so I could see the TV. On a number of occasions I saw Kordic making statements -- I did not hear anything but I, you saw him making a statement dressed in a camouflage uniform. These were excerpts of TV programmes. This is the table where we had lunch. The inmates of two cells never had lunch together, it was cell by cell. When we finished eating, then the people from the next cell would be allowed to eat. On this other side was the stove which heated the whole prison, and just underneath the window is a bed where HVO members would rest and who would talk until late into the night about their accomplishments, about their killings and lootings in the village around Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please mark -- you identified the room in which the guards were. Could you please, using a highlighter, mark that room with the letter "B"? (Witness marked photograph). And also the table at which you had meals with the letter "C". (Witness marked photograph). Thank you. Now, witness, could you please describe the size of the cell -- the cell to which you were put into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but I think it was about four metres by 360. I just know that 13 of us could not lie down on the kind of bed that existed, but that two of us slept on the concrete. We had blankets and we slept on those blankets on the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the kind of bed that existed inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a wooden bench, stretching from one wall to the other, and I must say that when we first came to the cell we lifted all the blankets there were in the cell and we found a knife and we called in a guard to show him the knife. This was probably planted there by a -- by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any heating inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just this stove, which was in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any electric lights inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not inside the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were brought to Kaonik, could you describe to this court what happened immediately upon being brought into the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were brought to the cell, the colleagues asked me, because I was in the police, for my advice, and I said to them, "I have never been a prisoner. I did imprison others". But I suggested to them that we should remove all the objects from the bed, that we shake out the blankets, and, when you are looking into the cell from the door, on the right-hand side towards the end was this knife, so we knocked on the door, the guard came, and he later brought in the commander -- the commander of the shift -- a young man, who had come, just before the conflict, from Canada. At first he shouted at us, thinking it was our knife and then we said, "But you searched us; you saw we had nothing on us," so, he took the knife. We arranged the cell a little bit. Then they brought in a tin to be used for urination in the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was this commander of the shift wearing at the time he came into the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A camouflage uniform. He did not have boots on his feet, because one of his legs was injured, so he was walking around in slippers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were brought to the cell, did you have occasion to see or meet the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A couple of days later, he entered our cell, wearing a camouflage uniform, with his sleeves turned up, with a pistol at his belt, and he asked, "Who is Zlotrg Edib?", and I said it was me. Then introduced himself at Zlatko Aleksovski. He said that he had spoken to my sister and brother-in-law and that they had enquired about me and he asked me how I was and whether I needed anything. I was afraid that this may be a provocation. So I said that I was fine and I did not need anything. And he went off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to recognise Mr. Aleksovski if you see him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Due to the fact that I know that it is him -- I could hardly recognise him otherwise, because I saw him twice in my life for 10 or 15 minutes each time, though I later did see his photograph from his former workplace, but this photograph was taken when he was much younger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you just said that you saw him twice in the 10 to 15 days that you spent in the days that you spent in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you described an occasion on which he came into your cell -- was it the first occasion or the second occasion that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the first occasion. On the second occasion was when we were being released from prison. We had to sign a paper, a release paper, in his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, when you were detained in the camp, did you hear any beatings and screams and cries going on in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at all times of day and night one could hear blunt blows and moans, but we did not see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see or hear detainees being taken out of the camp on labour detachments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost every morning, Muslims were called out and, when a Muslim is called out, then he would say the number of cell he is in, then the cells would be opened and the people would come out. When they were called out, they would be told "Strane", "Kula", "Loncari" or wherever they were supposed to go, and we could hear them leaving the prison premises, but I did not see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether prisoners in the camp in Kaonik were subjected to interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From my cell, a guard came to call Alija Basic, who was director of the Sintevit factory in Vitez a plant belonging to Unis. When Alija came back, he said that Darko Kraljevic had interrogated him, together with two other members of the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the guard wearing when he came into the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have an insignia on his sleeves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They all had the insignia of the Croatian army, that is the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you spent in custody in the Kaonik camp, witness, did you have sufficient food to eat and water to drink and water to wash yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did have three meals a day, but it was a very poor quality. Before my arrest I weighed 96 kilograms, and on the 16th of April, when I left, I had 63 kilograms. The hygiene was terrible, there was just a toilet at the bottom of the prison that was used by all the prisoners, and a wash basin, so if you needed water, or if you wanted to go to the toilet, you had to knock on the door to indicate the name of the cell, and wait for the guard to come and unlock it. There was no other way you could go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for how long, witness, were you detained in Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the 5th of May until the 13th or 14th of May. On the 16th, we were exchanged and we were released a couple of days before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you released from the Kaonik -- when were you taken out of the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from there, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were again taken to the cinema hall of the Radnicki University in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were exchanged on the 16th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the circumstances under which your exchange was secured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the International Red Cross that mediated between the army and the HVO to arrange the exchange, because 13 or 14 of us were exchanged on this side, and a couple of Croats were exchanged, also. Anyway, the exchange was attended by a representative of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, after you were exchanged, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour, in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think that this is a good time for us to break. But I would like to take advantage of the opportunity to say something. I notice that in the public there are many young students, and I should like to greet you as the hope of humanity and to wish you welcome to the International Criminal Tribunal. So we are now going to have a 15-minute break. (11.52am) (A short break) (12.14pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor. Cross-examined by MR. MIKULICIC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good morning, I am Goran Mikulicic. I am Defence lawyer from Zagreb. I am representing the accused in this place. I will ask several questions and would you please answer them to the best of your recollection. Mr. Zlotrg, you described for us in the introduction the events in which you took part in April and May 1993. Let me take you back to your first arrest when you were taken to the Workers' University. You said that your name was registered on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who registered you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the HVO police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander was who commanded these people who registered you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know higher commanders but I do know that Anto Kovac was one of the commanding officers. He was later killed. I think he and another man were shift commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I will focus on the events relating to the Kaonik facility, because this is relevant for these proceedings. You said that you were brought to Kaonik. Who brought you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time or the second time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first time and then the second time as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the HVO police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time was on the 25th, in the morning around 12, half past 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second time was on 5th May in the afternoon around 4 o'clock. I did not have a watch on me, so I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. You have described for us that some kind of record was being kept at the Workers' University, that there were two agendas, a red one and a blue one; who took your names down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anto Kovac was the one who took our names in the red agenda and another person whose nickname was Butur did the other agenda. They were members of the HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, I will now show you the same photograph that has been already shown to you by the usher, and which has been admitted as Prosecution Exhibit P63. I would kindly ask the usher to put the photograph on the ELMO. Thank you. I would kindly ask the technicians to focus the camera so that we can see the whole photograph on the screen -- thank you. Mr. Zlotrg, on this photograph you identified two facilities and you have marked them with two letters. I would kindly ask you to use the pointer and to circle that part of the photograph which you believe represents the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the place Kaonik or the facility where we were detained?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, would you please circle the building in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my first time there, I was detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not only referring to buildings but the whole area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought in at night so I do not know exactly where it was. It used to be a military depot and it used to be premises. I could circle it for you, but it would be approximately, so before the conflict access was not allowed to these premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I do not wish you to circle something you are not sure about, but could you identify for us other facilities -- other buildings that can be seen on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can show you the location where the intervention squad of the Croatian Defence Council was located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, could you please show that to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness indicates on photograph). In this building here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark the building the same way you have marked buildings so far but using another letter, please? (Witness marked photograph). Mr. Zlotrg, how do you know that the intervention platoon of the HVO was located in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that, because our colleague from the cell Fuad Kaknjo spent one night there, and we had to pass by that building, which was situated 30 metres away from the entrance to the Kaonik facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Could you also identify other locations on the photograph? Do you know for which purpose they were used and what they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just know that the facility used to be a military depot, a military warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, you said that guards were wearing uniforms in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you also met the warden and later you came to know his name, Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, he introduced himself. How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was dressed in a camouflage uniform and he had a pistol in his belt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any insignia on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing a shirt and the shirt did not have any insignia and I did not see him wearing a jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, you said that you saw photographs of Zlatko Aleksovski; where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before he became a member of the HVO, he used to work at the Zenica correction facility. He used to be a deputy -- I do not know exactly which function he had, but he knows that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, was that prior to the events or after the events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see his photograph anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Mr. Zlotrg, was Zlatko Aleksovski commanding the military police or the intervention platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what kind of competencies he had, whether he was commander of the intervention platoon, but I know that he commanded -- the guards who guarded us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, my colleague from the Prosecution asked you whether you had heard any screams, moans, or some similar noise during your time at Kaonik. I will ask you a different question. Did you see any actions which would result in such noises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were locked up in the cell, and we did not have an opportunity to see anything, except for what was going on in our cell, but we could clearly hear the sounds coming from the surrounding cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, you said that you were given food three times a day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you maybe see what kind of food was given to the guards in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what they ate. I just know that we took meals after them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they use the same place to have their meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see them, I did not hear a noise coming from the use of cutlery -- because this was right across my cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how do you know that they did actually take meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I believe that no-one would have guarded me if they had not had anything to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, this is merely an assumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in order to live, you simply have to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, you obviously have some experiences as a policeman, so you have to tell me from your experience what guards were eating -- did you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see that, but the people who brought us food told us that the food was being prepared all together and what we had to eat was very hard pieces of meat, but the rest was simply water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, while you were at Kaonik, did you personally see any mistreatment or beatings of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, that is enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, when Fuad Kaknjo was returned to the cell, we noticed he had bruises all over. How he sustained them, we do not know. Maybe he had fallen down or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, thank you very much for your answers. I do not have any further questions. Re-examined by MR. MEDDEGODA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions that arose out of cross-examination. Witness, you were shown Exhibit 63, Prosecution Exhibit 63. You marked on the exhibit buildings with the letters "A" and "B", the buildings in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you, during your stay in Kaonik, taken to -- taken out of those buildings to any other building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, except for the first time I was there, when I was sent to dig trenches, when I was taken from this building here. (Witness indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever taken to the building where the intervention group was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not, but I know that Fuad Kaknjo spent the time after the interrogation in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I do not think that we have it on the record that the witness has identified the building of the intervention platoon of the HVO. It has been identified with a letter "F" -- I think it has to be confirmed -- do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your concern, your Honour. The Defence agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, we do not have any further questions for you. You have completed your testimony, and we would like to thank you once again for having appeared before this Tribunal, and we wish you a safe return to your country. Thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we still have a half hour before the lunch break. I should like to know whether you consider it useful for us to begin the next testimony, or should we have the lunch break now. What is your opinion, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in your hands as to what you find most convenient, but we are in a position to start with the next witness now and to continue after the luncheon break. I should say, though, your Honours, that this is the last witness for today; we will have another witness for tomorrow, but we have no other witnesses for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Perhaps, if he is the only witness for today, we could try and make an effort and then we would not meet in the afternoon at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not sure that we would be finished -- I do not think we would finish -- we will see how we go. We can try, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Let us try. I do not know whether the interpreters agree to prolong the morning a little, and then we would be free for the afternoon --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Then we will try. Could you have the witness brought in, please? (The witness entered court) Good morning, Sir. Do you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear you very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated. Thank you for having come to the International Criminal Tribunal, and, first, you will be answering questions put to you by Mr. Marchesiello of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. ENES SURKOVIC Examined by MR. MARCHESIELLO

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Surkovic. Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please start by stating your name, age and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Enes Surkovic. I was born on 2nd of March 1949 in Konjic. I am a Bosniak of ethnic origin. My religion is Islam, I am a member of the SDP, the Social Democratic Party and I am a graduate mechanical engineer. Most of my career I spent working as a teacher in Vitez, I was a teacher for about 20 years. I taught mechanical engineering in that school and I also spent some time involved in politics. For a time, I was a professional politician, and during my working lifetime, I was a manager -- a director of a secondary school, a manager of a factory in Vitez. Vitez, for me, is a very familiar town. I am very well versed in the political climate before the war. I am also familiar with the activities of the political parties during the war. I wish to declare here, with full responsibility, that before 1990, before the multi-party elections in Vitez, there were absolutely no conflicts. The Croats and Muslims lived in close relations amongst each other. As a teacher, I often went to the villages, I spoke to people there, and among the elders no-one recollected any nationalistic conflicts between Croats and Muslims in the past.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Could I ask you some questions? You mentioned -- in order to make the court more aware of some of the facts you have referred to, you said you were involved -- you were a member of the SDP Party. Can you explain, briefly, what the initials mean and which were the main characteristics, or are the main characteristics of this Party, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to make a correction. In 1980, I was President of the League of Communists for the municipality of Vitez. In those days, the leaders of the present-day republics, Mr. Kirog Gligorov, the President of Macedonia, Mr. Milan Kucan, Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, Mr. Bulatovic, all of them were members of the League of Communists. It is known only for Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, the President of Bosnia Herzegovina, was never a member of the League of Communists and he was persecuted in those days and spent some time in prison. I was President of the Party for four years in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt you, and I know that, as a policy-maker, you are deeply involved in that activity, and you have had a lot of experiences and facts and events that you are familiar with; but I would rather go and ask you about the facts and ask you to follow what I am going to ask you. I simply wanted you to explain to the court which were the main characteristics of the Party you were a member of and actually you were the President of that Party in Vitez. To start with, what do the initials "SDP" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the collapse of Tito's Yugoslavia, in Bosnia Herzegovina and in the other republics, a number of parties cropped up. Among them was the Social Democratic Party, a modern political Party with a European orientation, a Party advocating democracy, human rights, a market economy and, of course, a unified Bosnia Herzegovina. This political Party is open to Serbs, Croats and Muslims. It is not a single ethnic Party, but a multi-ethnic one and it is open to all people of goodwill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, I think that is enough. Could you please explain and tell the court how was the political situation in Vitez after the 1990 multi-Party election -- I am concerned particularly with the seats apportionment in the local Parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The new Parliament -- the Parliament formed after the first multi-Party elections, numbered 60 aldermen or deputies. In that Parliament the HDZ had 23 deputies; the SDA, 16; SDS, two; and the Opposition, which consisted of the SDP, the Reformists and the Liberals, we had 19 seats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In November 1991, the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna was established. Did the situation you described of the Muslim people in Vitez change significantly thereafter, compared to the Croat community situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the situation changed significantly. The newly formed political Parties interpreted democracy erroneously, I would say, in that -- and especially HDZ, because the word "democratic" implies democracy and, within a short period of time, the SDP Party, the SDA Party, the trade unions -- all of them were thrown out of their premises and these were occupied by the HDZ. People who did not agree with the HDZ, and among them were my friends, members of the SDP -- Ivanic Mijo, Stipo -- they are terrorised and one night they were taken from the SDP premises to the woods. They were shot behind their heads; they were threatened if they went to SDP meetings. I claim that at that time members of the Serb people, and there were only 5.4 per cent of the population were Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I am sorry for interrupting you. Could you slow down a little bit so that the interpreters can follow you, because we would like to understand everything that you are saying. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, Professor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, shall I continue -- may I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would rather ask you to describe to the court, how did the Muslim community react to this new and difficult, for them, situation -- very difficult, extremely critical situation, as you described it? How did the Muslim community react? Did they organise in some way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I pointed out a moment ago that there were no conflicts between the Muslims and Croats in Vitez in the past and the Muslims wanted to avoid conflict at all costs, and at the level of the Vitez municipality, a council was set up for the protection of the interests of the Muslims. I was not a member of that council, but my friends were -- Dr. Mujezinovic, Mr. Fuad Kaknjo and others were members of this council. Whenever an incursion occurred into a Muslim house, and there were cases of people being beaten up -- for example, Mr. Dzevad Ridzanovic, who had an MA in technology, he was beaten up in front of his wife and children, a sack was thrown over his head, he was taken out of his flat to the woods and he spent two days and two nights in custody. Mr. Fuad Salkic, an MA in electrical engineering, he was also taken. Private shops and kiosks owned by Muslims were blown up; monuments from the past; a bust of a revolutionary, Mose Pijade, a man who was a fighter against fascism, who was very prominent in the Second World War, his bust was broken up and blown up, and the Muslim Council, the Council for the Protection of Muslim Interests, reacted by issuing statements, and making those statements on Croatian television in Vitez. I must admit that these statements were correctly read out on television, but nothing came of it all. There was little use -- little benefit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let us go to your personal experience and I would be grateful if you could tell the court what, briefly -- what happened to you and your family on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 16th April, I was in my flat at the time. I was working in the secondary school as a professor, and about 20 past 5, we were woken up by shell fire, mostly mortar fire and light infantry weapons could be heard. We went into the basement. The lights were on, however, there were no tenants there. Obviously, somebody had come there earlier on, unlocked the door and switched on the light.
