As we were alone, we went back to our apartment. 20 minutes or so later, I was looking through the window and I saw a flame in Stari Vitez, obviously houses were on fire. From the direction of Ahmici, one could hear artillery fire, probably mortars were operating there and there was a fire that could be heard from Stari Vitez as well. I went down to the basement again with my family and, this time, there were many tenants there -- almost all of them were there, women and children, both Croats and Muslims. All of us were frightened. Both the Croatian and the Muslim women were crying, because it was obvious that we had war and that the situation was getting more and more complicated. About 6 o'clock, some young men knocked on the door wearing camouflage uniforms. A Croatian woman, a neighbour of mine, opened the door. I wanted to open it, but she said, "No, you will not open it, I will open it." We were in the basement, and these two young HVO men came to the door, and told us that the men should go and unlock their apartments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Professor, could you describe these soldiers in camouflage. Did they have something on their face -- did they wear masks or something similar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot describe them. Let me continue. I turned towards my apartment door. When I got hold of the handle, the door was unlocked and I was surprised to see in my kitchen a man in a camouflage uniform with a black stocking over his face. You could just see his eyes, there were slots for his eyes. He was tall wearing a camouflage uniform. Next to him was my older son -- these local people of Vitez covered themselves up with masks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was your son at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son was 15 at the time -- my older son who was there. He was a secondary school pupil. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the order was for the men to unlock the doors, I called my son over, because I saw that this man had an automatic rifle on him. And I must point out that, before that, this young man standing there had broken the door on the cupboard in the kitchen with his rifle, and I had a pistol in that cupboard and this was locked, because of my children, but I had a permit for that pistol. My oldest son told me later that he had asked the soldier for permission to go downstairs and get the key for the cupboard, but he would not let him, so he broke the door and this man had looked through my papers and my documents. He was obviously looking for something and I was scared for my child. So I said to Denis -- and that was my son's name -- "Go to the basement." This young man was obviously surprised, because, after all, they were not sure of themselves. They were in another person's apartment, and he said, "No", the young man could not -- the child could not go downstairs, but I begged him to let him go because I was afraid he would get killed. I insisted that he go down and this masked man took his automatic rifle, he cocked it, pointing it at me and said he would kill me. I tried to remain as cool as I could, and collected. I knew that this man probably knew him, because I had worked in the secondary school in Vitez for some 20 years. So I said to him, "Listen, young man, if you are looking for weapons, if you are looking for the pistol, I have put it away. Just let the boy go downstairs and keep me here." He asked me, "where is the pistol?", and I said that it was in the washing-machine where I had hidden it. The boy moved towards the bathroom where the washing-machine was. I pointed to my son, telling him to come out. I must point out that behind me was a Croat, my neighbour, Ilija Azinovic, who was ringing his hands and who kept saying, "please go downstairs, please go to the basement", as if he felt that something terrible would happen. My son went by me and I followed him. On the staircase I was met by another young man, who was not wearing a mask. He was about 180 centimetres tall, he had freckles, he was wearing an earring in one ear. He was not masked and I could recognise him if I were to see him. He passed by me. He reached my apartment. My neighbour, Ilija Azinovic, told me later, "Thank God the masked man entered your flat first. If it had been the other blond one, he would have killed you". I said, "Why would he do that? I do not believe he would have killed me." Mr. Azinovic said to me that this blond fellow, when I went down the stairs, took a rifle and pointed it at my back, he wanted to shoot, but the masked man had come out of the apartment in the meantime and he prevented him from doing that. My son and I went to the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have another question to put to you as to this moment. In your experience, was somebody killed during this episode in your basement -- actually killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I entered the basement we could hear rifle fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Perhaps in your testimony, you could make pauses, because the interpreters cannot follow you, so please make a pause when you come to the end of the sentence. Do you understand the need to slow down and to make a pause at the full stop -- can you continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course I understand. I can, but I think that you are probably tired and you want to get through this as quickly as possible, but I will slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Professor, I would like you not to comment and not to make these kind of comments, just answer my questions, possibly, and as the President told you, try to slow down in order to help the translators to do their job. Did you understand that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand, thank you. When we got to the basement, my boy and myself, we heard bursts of fire on the upper storeys of the building I lived in. My neighbour, Ms. Jasmina Omerdic, started crying. We asked her why she was crying. She said that her husband was not amongst us. We did not dare go upstairs to see what was happening. A couple of minutes later, we heard the sound of military boots on the steps. Obviously, HVO soldiers were leaving our building. Shortly after that, the entrance door banged shut. I asked my neighbour, Franjic, a Croat, to come with me to see Salih or Omerdic's flat, to see whether the man was alive. The man went with me for a couple of steps, but then he moved away from me, and said that he did not have the courage to go upstairs. A good friend of mine, Ilija Azinovic, offered to come with me, and we went to Salih Omerdic's apartment. Salih was killed. His head and shoulders were on the floor. His middle area and his pelvic area and his legs were on a couch. I saw on the right-hand side of his face a wound -- obviously, that was the entry wound of the bullet. I moved closer to him. I raised his head, and, from the other side of the head, that is, in the same direction, was a larger wound. I bent down over the man and I saw another wound on his neck -- as the head was leaning over to one side, I saw that this was a blow with a knife. The muscles of the neck had been cut. This part here (indicating) had not been cut. Therefore, this was a penetrating wound -- he had been stabbed. The man did not show any signs of life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go back to the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Ilija Azinovic and myself laid the man on the floor. I closed his mouth, and eyes. Then I buttoned up his collar below his neck, so that his wife, if she were to come to her apartment, would not see this wound in his neck. Then we covered him with a sheet. Another two neighbours came up then -- Professor Hajrudin Zisko and Emir Priganica -- they saw this, and all of us then went back to the basement. We had to let his wife know what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, I know how concerned you are with the facts I am examining you about and I do not want you to have the impression that we are pushing you ahead. I want you to have all the time you need -- you think necessary to tell what is relevant to the case, but even if it is important for you to say, we have to find a good measure as to this. So, do you think it will take you a long time to go ahead telling us your story from this point of view? . I am saying that, because, your Honours, I hope they will understand -- I think it is important for the witness not to have the impression that all what he has to say, and I personally will take care about the fact that everything he is saying is relevant to the case, but I think that psychologically he should not be put in the situation where he is urged to deliver his declarations, so I am sorry to say that, but I am afraid that we will have to -- I cannot maintain the promise I made to the court, and I think I will take it a little longer time to go ahead with this witness, if your Honours understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: No problem. You just promised to try.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, I think it would not be advisable to pressure the witness. It is just a question of organisation. The Trial Chamber is fully conscious of the fact that we should not exert any pressure on the witness. Therefore, I think it is better for us to have our luncheon break and then, in the afternoon, we can continue, calmly and quietly, and at ease, so we are going to have a lunch break now and we will resume work in the afternoon. (1.02pm) (The luncheon adjournment) 21 22 23 24 25 (2.30pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Is everybody ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The Prosecution has the floor. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Mr. Surkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not have the same impression this morning, but anyway, let me remind you that I will put the precise question on a matter of fact and I am expecting you to answer these questions. You have to know and realise that this is not in an historical or political context, or a sociological context -- it is a judicial context -- yes? So I will ask you some precise facts and please answer to them. Now, I left you in your apartment building in Zenica. Now, what I want to know and what the court wants to know is what happened after that -- where were you taken, if you were taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The apartment was not in Zenica -- I was talking about Vitez -- the apartment was in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, at about 10 o'clock, three HVO soldiers arrived. We were in the basement, and they ordered Croats, both men and women, to one side of the basement -- to go to one side of the basement and the Muslims to go to the other side of the basement. Both Croatian and Muslim women started crying, because a murder had already happened in the building and we did not know what was awaiting us. After that, an order came for the Muslims, both men and women, to take their children and go to the premises of the Workers' University.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you conducted there and by whom, if so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I just add something, please? Some women fainted. HVO soldiers asked me, because they recognised me, to tell them that we were only going to the Workers' University to sign a piece of paper and that no harm would be done to anyone, so these three HVO soldiers took us to the basement of the Workers' University.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which kind of situation did you find there? Were there other Muslim people gathered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once we got there, there were about 20 persons there -- there were women and children, and children 10 years of age. Dr. Ekrem Mahmutovic was there as well. The rest of us were all men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then, were the women and children sent back home later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: New groups of people were being brought in, including women and children, who were camped there for about four hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then women and children were released and sent back home, whereas men between the age of 16 and 70 and over remained there at the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a camp or a building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I say it was a camp. There was no barbed wire around it. However, we were not free -- it was not a usual prison. Those were premises in the basement, but the reason I am referring to it as a "camp" is because innocent people were being detained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand your point of view. How long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that camp, I remained until the 3rd of May 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which were the conditions within the Radnicki University?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have any blankets there, there were no beds. We were given a can of fish a day and a quarter of a loaf of bread. However, our families were allowed to bring us some food and some blankets as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay there, did you notice whether some of the prisoners were taken out of those premises, and for what reason, if so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three days later, we were allowed to, whoever wanted to go, to move to the cinema hall and to the upper storey and about 10 o'clock, 11 o'clock, groups of people were being taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all of them return on those occasions, or were some of them missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I used to work as a teacher, I knew many as young men, I remember Almir Gadjun, who used to be a student of mine, who never came back. The people who were there with him told us that he had been killed while digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After how many days did you leave the cinema where you had moved, and how many of you did leave the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, representatives of the BiH army and the HVO arrived and they told us that we would be released on the 1st of May and that we would be sent home. However, this did not take place, and there were about 85, 86 people at that time at the cinema hall. A number of them, perhaps 60 of them, did go home on the following day -- that is, on the 1st of May, whereas 23 of us remained at the cinema hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you leave the cinema hall -- those who had remained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 3rd of May, around 4 o'clock, 20 minutes past 4, Zlatko Nakic arrived in the cinema hall and he called names of certain detainees. He called out seven names, seven of us, and he ordered us to take our things and to get out to the corridor. They took us to a van, and they transported us from there to the chess club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names, or some of the names, of those who were with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember all of them -- Fuad Kaknjo was with us, an engineer; Bahtija Sivro; Suad Salkic, also an engineer; Edib Zlotrg, Alija Basic, and two more persons whose names I cannot remember right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, how many of you were taken to the chess club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seven of us were taken to the chess club from the cinema hall, and later on five more people from Vitez were brought to the chess club, all of them Muslims. One more man by the name of Sahman joined us later on. He had been at Manjaca, in one of the Chetnik camps and, after he was released, he came back to Vitez and then he was arrested again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Surkovic, were you able, in those circumstances, to send a message? You say that your relatives were allowed to visit you with food; were you able to have a message to your relatives delivered -- the fact that you were being brought away from the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suspected that something was wrong, because they had released a large number of people from the camp, and the 13 of us were transported to the chess club, so I had an inkling that something bad would happen, so I made a list of people, all 13 of us who were there at the chess club. I sent -- I gave that list to the wife of a colleague of mine, who was there with me at the camp, who happened to be passing under the window. Her last name is Karajko and her husband was there with me. He told her to bring him some food to the chess club, and on that occasion I gave her the list, and I asked her to take -- to make copies of that list and to give it to our families and to UNPROFOR and, if possible, to the command of the 325th Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, your assumption is that it was known you were being taken away from the cinema and brought to the chess club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, since -- at 4.30, 4.20am we were taken from the cinema hall, only seven of us from that camp, it was obvious that I could not expect anything good to happen to us, and also, in view of our previous experiences and considering the murders that had taken place in Vitez, and in view of certain provocations to my family, to my relatives; late night calls, the destruction of my property in Vitez and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand you were asked not to bring your things with you -- your belongings -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the chess club, we spent two days and two nights. When they took us from the chess club to Busovaca, it is true that Mr. Marko Vidovic answered to my question whether I shall take personal belongings, he said that we would not need anything there and that we should not take anything with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left -- on leaving the chess club, the HVO soldiers did not give you any indication about the place you were going to be taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not say anything to us and I had the feeling that they were doing it in secret -- in secrecy. A van arrived and Marko Vidovic called us out and told us to get on the van. The driver turned on the engine and we set off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said you did go to Busovaca, or Kaonik more precisely. How long did this trip take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This all happened five years ago and, to the best of my recollection, I believe that we set off around 10 o'clock on the 5th of May -- that we left the premises of the chess club. Kaonik is not very far from Vitez. However, when we got there in front of the former military warehouse at Kaonik, we did not get off immediately, but we stood -- we remained sitting in the van for about an hour, an hour and 20 minutes. We did not know why we were waiting, and what they planned to do with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we were ordered to leave the van, to get off, and we had to walk in a single file, one by one, to the premises of the former military warehouse that had been redone in the meantime. We were searched at the entrance. We had to take out all our belongings from our pockets and raise our hands so the HVO soldiers could search us. They then took us to cell number 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the interior of this building in which you were searched and then detained into cell number 13?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my estimate, it is a square building which is approximately 30 metres long. In front of the building was a kind of platform -- the kind they have at warehouses from where trucks are loaded. There was a large corridor running across the middle of the building and there was also a table with chairs, where we used to take our meals. Also, in the building, inside the building, was a large stove that had been made of a barrel -- an oil stove that heated all the premises inside the building, so that was at the entrance -- at the entrance of that particular building. On the right-hand side, there was an office of the police and, on the left-hand side, there was the office of Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: If I am permitted, I would like to introduce as evidence one photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is document exhibit number 65. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, can you look at the photograph which is on the ELMO and tell the court whether these are the premises you have been describing to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the area I have been describing. You can see the stove here and the table at which we took our meals (indicating), both lunch and dinner. Here on the sides (indicating), you can see doors. Here (indicating) was cell number 19 where prisoners were detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us and sign with a pen the office where the guards used to stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here on this photograph I cannot really recognise the office, but I know it was on the left side as you enter the building -- it was behind glass, so that those people could control movement. I do not remember very well and I cannot observe this particular detail on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you point to cell number 13 where you have been detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cell number 13 -- I believe it was behind the stove. As you get in here to the corridor (indicating), the police were on the right-hand side and, after the police office, the office of the police, was cell number 13. So, if the entrance is here (indicating), then cell number 13 should be thereabouts (indicating). So, the first door after the police -- after the office of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark with a pen and the letter "A" the cell number -- where you did locate cell number 13?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that this is the bed that used to be here (indicating). The police must have been here and I believe that behind this area here (indicating) was cell number 13. It was five years ago. I am not quite sure, but I believe it was there (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you be so kind as to draw a letter "A" near the cross you marked? (Witness marked photograph). Thank you. Do you remember something specific happening immediately after you were put into the cell? Did some sort of incident occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember an incident that occurred then, although it was some time ago -- we entered the cell and it was normal for us to tidy up the area a little bit. There was a wooden pallet there with a mattress and some blankets on it, but it was all messy, so we wanted to clean it up a little bit. The professor who was brought there with me, Kadir Dzidic, found a big knife under the blanket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what did you decide to do with this knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We then called the shift commander, and we showed him the knife. This gentleman was very angry when he saw the knife and he started shouting at the guards, and he wanted to know how the knife had ended up there, and one of those young men was honest and he said that he had forgotten the knife there by accident and the shift commander said that he would investigate the whole case and that this young man would be punished for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Surkovic, during your stay in Kaonik, you spent all your time in the cell -- you, personally -- did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, except for one day when I went to a medical examination -- I only stayed four days at cell number 13. Later on, I was transferred -- we were transferred to another cell where there was more room for sleeping, because in this other one there were 13 of us and that cell was only 15 or 16 square metres large, so they wanted to give us somewhat better accommodation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, during your stay in Kaonik, were some of you interrogated and who, if so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first amongst us was taken, I think, on the third day for interrogation -- his name was Serif Causevic. He is now deceased. He was taken about 6 o'clock in the afternoon. He stayed there for about four hours. When he came back from the interrogation, he was crying. We asked him did anyone beat him. He said they had not, but that the interrogation was very hard to bear. He said it was some sort of cross-examination; there were three investigators; he was extremely depressed. We thought he had been beaten up, but he said -- he denied it, but he just found the interrogation difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where had he been taken in order to be interrogated -- did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told us that they had taken him outside the building. To tell you the truth, he did say where, but I do not remember now -- I think he was taken to town, to the MUP premises, or the municipality. In any case, it was not there he was interrogated; he was taken somewhere by car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell who did call him out of the cell on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he not tell you anything about those investigators -- were they from the police, were they HVO, from the military police -- did he give you any indication about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that there was a highly experienced man among them, that he was a professional to all intents and purposes -- a man who must have worked in the judiciary before, who knew how to put the questions and who expected exhaustive answers. But he did not mention any names, because he did not know the people who interrogated him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who else was interrogated after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, engineer Fuad Kaknjo was taken for interrogation. He was kept there a long time. He did not come back the whole night, but I was not in his cell when he was taken away -- I was in cell number 9. But, later on, he told me that it was very hard for him, that we had a lot of problems. He said he was beaten during the interrogation and, when we left the camp, he still had some bruises on his body. After Fuad Kaknjo, engineer Bahtija Sivro went for interrogation and Basic Alija, and I do not think they took anyone else for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay there, were you visited by the Red Cross or by ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes -- there were two visits. The first was by the International Red Cross. They filmed the cells, they talked to us, they filmed us. We asked the International Red Cross to organise medical checkups for us and, also, for them to intervene and prevent us being taken to dig trenches, as we were afraid that someone might get killed there and I can confirm now that, out of our group, no-one was taken to dig trenches, and that the very next day we were taken to see a doctor for an examination, and whoever wanted to see a doctor was enabled to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the ECMM visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes -- they came, too. I remember that these men in cell number 9, and there were five of us, asked me to talk to them. We presented our comments in a nice manner so that our stay in Busovaca was facilitated by these visits, by the International Red Cross and the European Monitors. We felt freer, safer, we knew people knew where we were, and we did not expect anything bad to happen to us if the world knew where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the camp commander with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, he was not. I saw the camp commander only two or three times in my whole life. If necessary, I can explain when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, did you know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time, that is, the third day after we arrived in the camp, Mr. Aleksovski came in to cell number 13. He called out, asking for Edib Zlotrg. Zlatko introduced himself. He said he was the camp commander, Zlatko Aleksovski, and that he had come to convey to them a message from his relatives in Zenica. That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, was there another name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After the European Monitors left, Zlatko came by to cell number 9 once. He talked to us for a while and he offered people cigarettes. The third time was when we were about to leave to be exchanged, and I asked Mr. Aleksovski then for some of my things to be returned, which had been seized from me in cell number 9 by HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then when were you released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 14th of May orders came for us to be released, and for us to be exchanged. Clearly, we had to sign those orders and that was the third time I saw Mr. Aleksovski, because he told us this, and we were not released straight away, but we were taken back to Vitez. When we reached the cinema, we were told that we had to wait for half an hour for some HVO commanders to come for us, to sign some papers and that we would then be released. However, that was not what happened. We were held in the cinema for another two days and two nights, which means the 15th and the 16th, and it was only after that that we were released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did some meeting take place during your stay there, during those two days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One day -- I think it was the second day of our stay -- it was the 15th of May, two young HVO men entered the cinema and they called out Suad Salkic, an engineer, to come out. I asked whether anyone else should come with him and he said there was no need, because these were his acquaintances and neighbours from the village of Sadovaca. However, shortly after that we heard some strange sounds in the corridor. I opened the door and I saw that these two young HVO men were beating Suad Salkic with a wooden pole. The policeman on duty ran up and we also came out of the cinema hall, so that we grabbed engineer Salkic away and the policeman on duty started yelling at these two young men who had beat Salkic. One of them had hit him with this pole at the back of the head, so that he was bleeding. He was as white as the wall; he was terrified. We took him back into the cinema hall, and that was how the incident ended. Of course, I personally later informed Mr. Santic about this, as well as Mario Cerkez, Stipo Krizanac and Boro Zozic, who came to visit us two hours later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did they come to visit you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Ivica Santic, not being aware of this incident, proposed that we should not leave Vitez. He asked that we stay and that, within a period of two hours, they would return our apartment keys to us. I asked Mr. Ivica, "How safe will we be in our apartments and will we be protected adequately?" Mr. Ivica answered that we would be as protected and as safe as he and that we had nothing to fear and he asked us to stay, saying that, if we left Vitez, that many other people, including both Croats and Muslims with high qualifications, would leave Vitez, following our example. I turned Mr. Suad Salkic around and he was still bleeding at the back of his head and I asked him, "Is this the kind of safety you are guaranteeing for us?" They were extremely surprised to see the man bleeding so heavily, and I explained to them then what had happened. I said that we would not stay in Vitez -- under no circumstances -- and that, if they had really wanted us to stay, they would not have taken us to a camp, deprived us of our freedom, and I also said, "If you do not let our families go with us, then we will protest, too, and we will not move from here." I wish to point out that I had learned previously from people who had passed through this area, from Croats, my friends -- and I stressed that every Muslim family had at least five or six Croat friends, so there were decent honourable people -- and I learned that my family had already been moved to Zenica but not the families of my friends and that is why I insisted that our families should go with us, that is, the families of the other people who were with me in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, when were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 16th of May, about 12 o'clock in the village of Poculica, the exchange took place. We were taken to Zenica with our families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you surely have questions to put to the witness. Cross-examined by MR. MIKULICIC

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do have some questions, your Honour, but not too many. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Goran Mikulicic, I am an attorney and I represent the accused in this case together with my colleague, Mr. Joka, sitting next to me. I should now like to ask you a number of questions and I would ask you kindly to answer them to the best of your recollection. Mr. Surkovic, in view of your previous life that you have described to us, you were a prominent figure in Vitez and the surroundings. What I mean is that you knew many people and many people knew you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Similarly, during these critical events that we are discussing, that is, the first half of 1993, you had contact with some quite important people in the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, did you ever have any contact with Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Aleksovski in Busovaca three times and I knew nothing about him from before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you saw Mr. Aleksovski for the first time in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have described to us the events, your arrival at Kaonik, and the entrance to the building where you were put up. Do you remember whether, at the entrance to the building, there was any kind of board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recollect that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there were locks on the doors of the cells where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The door could only be opened outwards. We could not open the door from the inside, but, if we needed anything, we had to knock, and the guard on duty would remove a kind of lid that was on the door, he would peep inside and ask us what we wanted and then he would open the door from the outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how he opened the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the door, there was a kind of latch, a kind of lever, which was lifted (indicating) and on the door frame was another latch and that is how the door could be opened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Surkovic, that, in addition to people of Muslim origin, there were people of other ethnic origins?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember very well that one evening, about 10 o'clock, a Croatian soldier was brought to cell number 9. His name was Zoran. He was a bit tipsy -- he was under the influence of alcohol. He was very talkative. He had no weapons on him. He told us that he had fled from the front, that the fighting was fierce, and that he had somehow found a bottle of spirits. He had drunk it, he had been caught by the HVO police and they had brought him to cell number 9. If you need any more details, I can go into them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that is fine, Mr. Surkovic. Mr. Surkovic, you said that during your stay in Kaonik you saw Zlatko Aleksovski on three occasions; do you remember how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was dressed in a camouflage uniform, but I did not notice any ranks indicated on the uniform of Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Surkovic. Thank you, your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, I have a question. At one point, you said that you asked Mr. Aleksovski for the property which had been taken away from you previously by the HVO; did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you did, you understood me very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Did Mr. Aleksovski say anything to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksovski was very angry when I said that HVO soldiers had entered the cells on a number of occasions and they had indeed entered, and that, on one occasion, they had taken some of our personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But did Mr. Aleksovski give you back your property? What was his answer to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gentleman was very angry when he learnt about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But why was he very angry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that HVO soldiers had entered the cells on a number of occasions and they had mistreated some of the prisoners and, on top of that, they had taken some of my personal belongings. He said that this should not have happened. He appeared to be astonished, because these people who, with me in the camp, knew that my family was in Vitez, that my apartment had been destroyed, my car had been destroyed and everything, but this was something I cared about, I cherished, so I did -- I decided that I wanted to get it back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, you have completed your testimony here at the International Criminal Tribunal. We wish to thank you for coming, once again, and we wish you a safe journey home. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think that we have some other witnesses for today, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honours, there are no more witnesses for today. We have another witness for tomorrow, but not for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, we meet again tomorrow. (The witness withdrew) (3.26pm)
